summary:
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults. Section 146 of the criminal code, the British-inherited buggery offence, carries up to 10 years' imprisonment; section 148, gross indecency, carries up to 5 years. These colonial-era provisions remain in force.

On 16 February 2024 the High Court dismissed a constitutional challenge and upheld the ban, holding that outlawing homosexual activity is lawful. Same-sex conduct therefore stays criminal in the country. On 19 February 2024 the Eastern Caribbean rights alliance ECADE condemned the ruling, stating that LGBTQ+ Vincentians face greater vulnerability as a result.

No visa, entry-screening or admission rule affecting LGBTQ travellers is recorded in the sources, and no law governing gender markers on travel or identity documents is sourced here. The sources likewise record no provision on restroom or facilities access and no prohibition on gender-affirming care for visitors. These gaps reflect the sourcing, not a finding of permissive rules.

Violence risk is documented. Human Rights Watch reported on 20 July 2023, in the 58-page report 'They Can Harass Us Because of the Laws', that LGBT people in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines face bias-motivated violence and discrimination in daily life. In April 2019 Leswan Stewart, a cross-dressing gay teenager, was assaulted in a transphobic attack and then prosecuted for fraud on the allegation that he had pretended to be a woman; the prosecutor withdrew the charge in May 2019 without stating a reason. In September 2018 three cross-dressing young men were physically attacked.

Protection machinery is thin. The legislation addresses neither discrimination nor harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so LGBTQ people have no statutory basis on which to claim protection when they speak out. No associations or organisations dedicated to LGBTQ people exist in the country, and no helpline or help centre for LGBTQ youth operates. The country does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples receive none of the rights given to married couples. The Prime Minister has said any change to the law would be an OECS-wide decision, because constitutional and legislative provisions are similar across member states.

The sources record no enforcement figures for these offences, so the practical exposure of a visitor to prosecution cannot be quantified from this inventory.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's July 2023 report, drawn from interviews with LGBT people in the country, recommends decriminalising gay sex and enacting non-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity. Its documentation of everyday harassment is the principal evidence base for the hostility a visibly LGBTQ visitor may encounter outside formal legal channels.

Public expression has drawn threats. In September 2011 an article titled 'Not Easy Being Gay in St. Vincent and the Grenadines', written by a same-sex couple and published in the local magazine Vinci Kallaloo, drew more than 3,400 hits and over 50 comments within a day, several of them violent and murderous threats. In 2011 three lecturers at the St. Vincent and the Grenadines Community College were targeted by the college's director in what was described as an orchestrated scheme accusing them of 'homosexual tendencies', allegedly to remove political opponents.

The law has produced exile. Two men left the country because of the legislation; in their 2019 affidavits the constitutional petitioners stated that the legislation had exiled them from the country through its severely draconian and damaging effects. Javin Johnson, 22, was granted asylum in the United Kingdom in 2017 after establishing that he could not live as a gay man in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Sean Macleish, 53, a Vincentian resident of Chicago, publicly urged the Prime Minister to remove the laws so that he could return home with his partner, without effect.

The September 2018 attacks on three cross-dressing young men drew a response from Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves, who condemned the violence, called such homophobia unacceptable and called for an open national conversation on homosexuality. Official condemnation of discrete incidents has not translated into legislative change, and the constitutional challenge was lost in February 2024.
localsOnly:
Social infrastructure for LGBTQ residents is thin. There are no associations or organisations dedicated to LGBTQ people and no helpline or help centre for LGBTQ youth, so dedicated support and care access is absent for residents. The Caribbean HIV/AIDS Alliance is the main contact point for men who have sex with men.

Many gay men marry women and live down-low as a result of the legal and social environment, and LGBTQ life in the country is described as invisible and stigmatised. Residents who speak out about their circumstances have no statutory non-discrimination or harassment protection to invoke, since the law addresses neither.

Residents in same-sex relationships have no recognised standing: the country does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnership, and same-sex-headed households are ineligible for the rights afforded to married couples. For residents, the Prime Minister's position is that reform would have to be taken collectively, as an OECS-wide decision, rather than by Saint Vincent and the Grenadines alone.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory carries no enforcement data for sections 146 and 148: no arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction figures are recorded, so the practical likelihood that a visitor is charged for consensual private conduct is unresolved on these sources.

A Human Dignity Trust page documenting Eastern Caribbean constitutional challenges could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so the comparative litigation record for the wider Eastern Caribbean, including outcomes in other member states, is unresolved here.

The inventory states that 'healthcare, medication, and HIV services are not covered' without identifying which coverage scheme or eligibility category is meant; the meaning of that claim for a visitor seeking treatment is unresolved and should be verified against current health-service rules before it is relied on.

No source in this inventory addresses gender markers on passports or other identity documents, entry or visa rules keyed to gender presentation, facilities or restroom access, or requirements applying to gender-affirming medication carried across the border. These are gaps in sourcing rather than confirmed absences of regulation.
